sm: Lauren Zibo of the Atlas Society opens episode 329 of Objectively Speaking with senior scholar Stephen Hicks. Hicks says the Enlightenment is attacked by both the far left and the new right, which blame it for modern ills, including leftism, Hitler and the French Revolution. He wants to compare the Scottish and French Enlightenments, since the right often calls the French one bad and the Scottish one redeeming. He starts with the American founding, noting that John Locke was the most cited political thinker and that Adams, Jefferson and Madison all read him closely.

Hicks says the founders also read the French thinkers. Jefferson admired Montesquieu on separation of powers, Voltaire on religious toleration, and Turgot on early free-market ideas. But each founder also had a Scottish connection. Jefferson's teacher William Small at William and Mary was Scottish. Adams was introduced to Hutcheson, Hume, Lord Kames and Adam Smith by his legal mentors. Madison studied under the Scottish president of Princeton, John Witherspoon. Hicks concludes the founders were steeped in the English Enlightenment and the newer Scottish one, which came about two generations after the English.

Hicks explains that the Scottish Enlightenment grew out of the 1707 union with England, which brought wealth and energy and revitalized Scotland's universities. He dates its start to the late 1740s, with Hume's Inquiry in 1748, followed by Hutcheson in 1755, Smith in 1759, Kames in 1762 and Reid in 1764. He says it is downstream from English figures like Locke, Newton and Bacon. The French Enlightenment began earlier, in the 1720s, with Montesquieu's first work in 1721.

Hicks says Montesquieu and Voltaire both went to England to learn from it, and Voltaire's letters on England appeared in 1733. By the 1740s a large French generation was producing the vast Encyclopedia, edited by Diderot from 1751. His chronology is England first, France second, Scotland third and America fourth. He notes Scots were more serious because of Calvinism, and that Scotland had 1.2 million people against about 24.6 million in France, so France had a much deeper bench. He then raises the argument that French rationalist hubris explains the Revolution going bad.

Hicks says he does not find that argument very good, but it contains a grain of truth. Scottish thinkers lean toward common-sense realism, empiricism and modest skepticism, with Hume the most skeptical and Reid a common-sense realist. The French include skeptics and empiricists too, but also many rationalists who deduce universal principles a priori and apply them top-down to remake society. In the Q&A he calls Francis Hutcheson underappreciated. Hutcheson is associated with early utilitarianism and moral sentiment theory, and he was among the first Scots to condemn slavery in the 1750s.

Hicks says Hutcheson is overlooked because later thinkers developed his ideas more fully, such as his student Adam Smith, and later utilitarians like James Mill and John Stuart Mill. Asked about Hume, he says there are two Humes. As a philosopher he is a total skeptic and so a counter-enlightenment figure. As a writer on history, law, economics and politics he acts as a common-sense realist. Asked which Enlightenment thinker Objectivism most resembles, he says Locke, for political philosophy, church-state separation and toleration, though Objectivism is more original in metaethics.

Hicks says Locke anticipates Objectivism in his hedonism, his empiricism and his view that people are born with a clean slate, though Locke's representational theory of perception is an error. He calls Objectivism a smorgasbord of Enlightenment ideas plus original points, with Ayn Rand's fiery rhetoric closer to Voltaire and Diderot. Asked to compare the American and French revolutions, he says the American one was the purer culmination of Enlightenment philosophy because the colonists started from scratch. He argues there were two French revolutions. The first, from 1789 to 1791, was a success, and Lafayette drafted the Declaration of the Rights of Man and the Citizen with Jefferson's help.

Hicks says the first French Revolution applied English and American ideals of liberty, equality, property rights and religious freedom. By late 1791 and 1792 the liberals were outmaneuvered by radicals such as Robespierre, Danton and Marat, who followed Rousseau, whom Hicks calls anti-Enlightenment. They favored the general will, a mandatory national religion and collective merging of individuals, which led to the guillotine and mass executions. Asked about Nietzsche, he says Nietzsche is an anti-Enlightenment thinker and, though not a system builder, has a kind of organic unity in his ideas.

Hicks says Nietzsche rejects every major Enlightenment theme, including objective reality, reason, individualism, free will and equal rights. Asked about Joseph de Maistre, he says the early-1800s French thinker held a dark view of human nature and thought liberalism naive. He adds that the most influential current counter-Enlightenment figures are Foucault and Derrida, who are deep in philosophy and epistemology. For closing thoughts, he urges listeners to read Hutcheson, whose short work on morality is more accessible, and to remember the order of English, French, Scottish and American. Lauren thanks him and previews next week's guest, Hans Zeiger of the Jack Miller Center, on America's 250th birthday.
